It's useful to think of Heinlein's writing career as consisting of three periods - "early", "middle" and "late". He is most accessible in his early period, wrote most controversially in his middle period, and is most lovable, to those who know him well, in his late period.

I suggest you start with his "early period". During this time he wrote a great many important short stories, which have been collected into the several volumes of the "Future History" series. I suggest reading "The Man Who Sold the Moon", "The Green Hills of Earth" and "Revolt in 2100" from this series: all of these are collections of very readable SF stories.

Also in his early period, Heinlein wrote a large number of "juvenile" novels, each of which was published by Scribner's, generally in time to be Christmas presents for teenage boys. Everyone has their own favorites from this period: mine are "The Rolling Stones" (published in the UK as "Space Family Stone", by analogy with "Swiss Family Robinson") and "Tunnel in the Sky". The most critically acclaimed juvenile seems to be "Have Spacesuit, Will Travel".

Heinlein's "middle period" is characterised by more experimental writing styles, attempts to investigate alternative political systems through thought experiments, and the beginning of an awareness of human mortality. From this period I suggest you try "Stranger in a Strange Land" and "The Moon is a Harsh Mistress", as contrasting views of how society might be organised. My personal favorite from this period is "The Moon is a Harsh Mistress".

It's worth noting that somewhere in the 1960s Heinlein seems to have become aware of his own mortality, this knowledge being exacerbated by a case of peritonitis at the end of the decade. After this illness Heinlein seems to have wrestled with the prospect of death in several subsequent works. This preoccupation marks the start of his "late period": I'd say it this period begins with "I Will Fear No Evil". Some readers find his works from the 70s difficult. Others (including me) find him to be at his most human in his late period.

What comes over very strongly in the first two novels of Heinlein's late period - "I Will Fear No Evil" and "Time Enough for Love" - is his great fear of death. Both these novels are imaginative attempts to find technological solutions to the inevitability of death. By his third novel of this period he has given up on technological cures for death, and instead considers a way of escaping into the timeless and partially death-free worlds of fiction. Many readers find these three novels, particularly the first, very difficult to read. For me, though, they show Heinlein at his most open: when I read them I find myself feeling a tremendous tenderness towards a man who is so terribly, terribly afraid. Don't start with any of these novels, because until you have developed a love for Heinlein as a person (which you will as you read his earlier works) you will not enjoy them.

By the fourth novel of his late period, "Friday", Heinlein has, after a decade of brooding about death, come to terms with it and is back to his earlier form. "Friday" and "Job: A Comedy of Justice" are late gifts from a master story-teller. They are to Heinlein what the "The Winter's Tale" and "The Tempest" are to Shakespeare: stories that hint that they will become tragedies, but are subverted by their generous aging authors to happy endings. Just as Prospero can be read as a version of Shakespeare, so Alex in "Job" can be read as a version of Heinlein, and Alex's love for Margrethe in the novel mirrors Heinlein's own devotion to his wife Ginny. The last couple of Heinlein's late novels are best read as the dreams of an old man by the fire: loved by his fans, but not much appreciated outside that select band.

I notice that I've written most about Heinlein's late period. As you can tell, I have loved Heinlein for decades, and his work has had a huge influence on me, so it's natural for me to do this, because in his late period Heinlein is most open about himself in his writing. For me, his late period is like listening to the long wise conversations of a much-loved uncle: we forgive him his occasional rambles and repetitions because of our long relationship, in which he has encouraged us and chastised us in equal measure. For us, the loving, Heinlein's late period is wonderful. For a newcomer, though, this is not the best place to start. Start with a couple of his juveniles, and gradually read along with him as he grows. As he grows into full maturity, so will you.

I began my Sci-fi journey at the tender age of 13 reading my first Heinlein novel, Glory Road. Slighty racy, witty and charming, the Dean of Science Fiction pulled me into the world of sci-fi and fantasy. My favorite Heinlein novels are: Citizen of the Galaxy (also a brilliant audiobook read by the great Lloyd James), Farnham's Freehold (another fantastic audiobook read by Fred Major), and Orphans of the Sky and of course, the aforementioned Glory Road. On occasion Mr.Heinlein would weave his political beliefs not too subtly into his novels as well as some sexy bits here and there.

I highly recommend Larry Niven's Ringworld and The Mote in God's Eye.
